content.seoDescription: Read an original flash-fiction story inspired by a public writing-prompt API, plus a craft breakdown of implication, compression, and point of view.

blocks.text: This piece answers a short writing prompt about judgment and generosity published in the DummyJSON placeholder-content API. The prompt is used here only as a starting image; none of its wording or plot is reproduced below.

Marisol had transcribed four hundred trials before she let herself have an opinion about one of them. Her mother used to say that judgment was a debt paid twice: once when you made it, and once when it turned out wrong. Marisol had built her career on not paying it at all. She sat in the same chair every day, fingers moving over keys, turning voices into a record no one read until it mattered. She was not supposed to react. She was furniture with a skill.

The defendant that Tuesday was nineteen, and his hands shook so hard the bailiff had to steady the water pitcher for him. He kept saying he didn't remember driving the car, and the prosecutor kept saying that didn't matter, and Marisol kept typing both of those things down at exactly the same speed, because speed was the whole job. It was the third recess before she noticed her own hands had stopped moving.

She thought about the ice on Route 9, and the way her mother used to slow the car to a crawl every winter without explaining why, and how Marisol used to think that caution was just a story her mother told herself to feel careful. When the verdict came, she typed it exactly as spoken, no faster, no slower. Then she went home and, for the first time in eleven years at that courthouse, wrote down what a record could never hold: that some hands shake from guilt, and some shake from cold, and a transcript cannot tell you which.

National Flash Fiction Day, the organization that runs one of the form's longest-running annual celebrations, treats the short-short story as a distinct craft rather than a shrunken short story, built around a single scene doing more work than its length suggests. Marisol's story leans on that idea: everything happens in one recess, in one chair, inside one job she has done thousands of times.

The Flash Fiction Institute, which runs an annual flash-writing project built around daily prompts, defines flash fiction as a complete story told in well under a thousand words. That ceiling forces a writer to choose one turn, not several, which is why this piece resolves through a single physical detail: hands that stop moving.

Flash fiction's compression, as the Flash Fiction Institute's own guidance to writers emphasizes, works through omission as much as through what is written. This story never explains the verdict, the mother's history, or what Marisol writes down at the end. That withholding is the point: the reader is asked to sit with the same uncertainty Marisol cannot transcribe away.
Is this story based on a real case?
No. It is original fiction written for this Signal Fiction series in response to a public API prompt, not a report of an actual trial or person.
It is a complete, self-contained story told in a very small space, generally well under a thousand words, where every sentence has to carry more than one job.
